summary: A country on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean, founded in 1948 as the nation-state of the Jewish people. Jerusalem is a holy city of Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and the country is known for technological innovation.

ranking.name: Judaism
ranking.description: Israel is a Jewish state founded in 1948 on Zionist principles. The 1950 Law of Return allows Jews from around the world to immigrate and obtain citizenship, and Holocaust survivors, Jews from the Middle East and North Africa, and Soviet Jews in the 1990s arrived in large numbers. Judaism is very diverse internally, from ultra-Orthodox to secular, and many regard being "Jewish" as a nationality rather than a strict religious practice.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: After the Arab conquest in the 7th century the inhabitants of Palestine were gradually Islamized. During the 1948 war large numbers of Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled, and about 150,000 who remained became Israel's Arab citizens. Most are Sunni Muslims, concentrated in Galilee, the Bedouin areas of the Negev and the "Triangle", and their higher fertility rate keeps their share at about one fifth.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity originated in this land, and the deeds of Jesus in Nazareth, Bethlehem and Jerusalem make it a holy land. Most of Israel's Christians are Arabs, belonging to the Greek Orthodox Church and the Eastern-rite Catholic Church (Melkites), concentrated in Nazareth and Haifa; there are also Orthodox Christians who came with the Soviet immigration of the 1990s.

ranking.name: Druze faith
ranking.description: The Druze faith is a distinctive monotheistic religion that split off in the 11th century from the Ismaili branch under Egypt's Fatimid dynasty; its doctrines are kept secret and it does not accept converts. The Druze live mainly in villages in Galilee and on Mount Carmel, and since 1956 their men have performed Israeli military service at the request of their own community leaders, giving them a closer relationship with the Jewish state than other Arab groups.

religion.background: This land is a shared holy land of Judaism, Christianity and Islam: Jerusalem has the Western Wall, remnant of the Jewish Temple, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Al-Aqsa Mosque. After Rome destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE, most Jews were scattered across the world; after the Arab conquest in the 7th century, the local population gradually became mainly Muslim. With the rise of the Zionist movement in the late 19th century, Jewish immigrants returned to Palestine one after another, Israel was founded in 1948, and the Law of Return (1950) allowed Jews worldwide to immigrate. Today Israel is predominantly Jewish, but also has minorities such as Arab Muslims, Christians and Druze, and religion and national identity are closely intertwined.

language.official: The official language is Hebrew; Arabic has a special status.

ranking.name: Hebrew
ranking.description: From the late 19th century Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and Zionist educators revived Hebrew as an everyday language, and in 1922 the British Mandate authorities listed it as one of the official languages. After independence the government, through language schools and schooling, required immigrants from Europe, the Middle East, Ethiopia and elsewhere to learn Hebrew, making it the common language of the vast majority of Israelis.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic is the mother tongue of Israel's Arab citizens, about one fifth of the population; Arab schools teach in Arabic, and road signs are often in Arabic as well. It was one of the official languages from the British Mandate period, but the 2018 Nation-State Law downgraded it to a language with a "special status", and many Jewish families of Middle Eastern and North African origin still understand Arabic dialects.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Around the collapse of the Soviet Union, in 1989 and through the 1990s, about a million Soviet Jews and their family members immigrated to Israel under the Law of Return, the largest wave of immigration in Israel's history. The Russian they brought formed a distinct cultural sphere in newspapers, television and political parties, and Russian is heard especially often in cities such as Ashdod, Ashkelon and Haifa.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: Britain ruled Palestine from 1917 to 1948, and English was an official language of the Mandate; although it ceased to be official after independence, schools teach English from primary school, and it is widely used in the high-tech industry and academia. Native English speakers are mainly immigrants from the United States, Britain, South Africa and elsewhere.

language.history: Hebrew was spoken in ancient Israel and gradually ceased to be an everyday spoken language after the 2nd century CE, but for nearly two thousand years it remained the written language of Jewish prayer, scripture study and scholarship. In the late 19th century Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and others pushed to revive Hebrew as an everyday spoken language, promoting it in Jewish schools and settlements in Palestine; it is the only "dead language" in the world to have been successfully revived. After independence in 1948 the government set up language schools (ulpan) to teach new immigrants Hebrew, giving immigrants from over a hundred countries a common language. Arabic was originally an official language alongside Hebrew, but the 2018 Nation-State Law changed it to a language with a "special status", provoking controversy.

ranking.name: Hummus
ranking.description: Boiled chickpeas are pureed with tahini, lemon juice, garlic and olive oil and scooped up with pita. It is often topped with whole chickpeas, sauteed mushrooms or boiled eggs, and is an everyday meal for Israelis.
ranking.history: Chickpeas have been grown in the Levant for thousands of years, but the earliest clear recipes for hummus with tahini appear in Arabic cookbooks of around the 13th century (the broad picture is still disputed). After Israel's founding, hummus became a national food through the blending of the cuisines of Arab and Middle Eastern Jewish immigrants, and the specialty shops on the streets (hummusiya) often open only until midday. Israel and Arab countries such as Lebanon have long argued over hummus's "nationality", which also reflects the politics of food and national identity.

ranking.name: Falafel
ranking.description: Soaked chickpeas (or fava beans) are ground with herbs and spices, shaped into small balls and deep-fried, often stuffed into pita with salad and tahini.
ranking.history: Falafel is generally thought to originate in Egypt, where Coptic Christians made fried bean cakes from fava beans in place of meat during fasting periods, and it later spread to the Levant, where chickpeas were used instead. In the 1950s Jewish immigrants from Yemen and other Middle Eastern countries sold falafel in pita on the streets of Israel; cheap and vegetarian, it quickly became Israel's national street snack. But Palestinians and other Arab countries also regard it as their own tradition, which likewise stirs a "food appropriation" controversy.
ranking.imageCredit: Popo le Chien・CC BY-SA 3.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Shakshouka (eggs in tomato sauce)
ranking.description: Eggs are cracked into a spicy sauce stewed from tomatoes, sweet peppers and onions and cooked until set, then sprinkled with cumin and paprika and eaten by dipping bread. The whole skillet is usually brought to the table, and people dip bread into the sauce and eat together.
ranking.history: Shakshouka originated in North Africa, around Tunisia and Libya, and its name in Arabic dialects means "mixed together". Tomatoes and chili peppers came from the Americas and reached North Africa only after the 16th century via Spanish and Ottoman trade, so the dish took shape relatively late. In the 1950s–60s large numbers of Tunisian, Libyan and Moroccan Jews immigrated to Israel and brought it with them, and today it has become a signature dish of Israeli breakfasts and cafes.

ranking.name: Sabich (eggplant pita)
ranking.description: Pita stuffed with fried eggplant slices, boiled eggs, hummus, tahini, Israeli salad and mango pickle sauce (amba).
ranking.history: Sabich originates in the Sabbath breakfast custom of Iraqi Jews: because lighting a fire is forbidden on the Sabbath, they would fry eggplant and slow-cook eggs in advance on Friday and eat them cold on Saturday morning. In the 1940s–50s large numbers of Iraqi Jews immigrated to Israel, and at street stalls in places such as Ramat Gan they stuffed these ingredients into pita and sold them, which formed sabich. There are several accounts of the name's origin, one being that it comes from the Arabic word for "morning" (sabah).

ranking.name: Israeli salad
ranking.description: A light salad of finely diced tomatoes, cucumbers and onions seasoned with olive oil, lemon juice and salt. Its taste is tangy and refreshing, and it is often eaten at breakfast or with grilled meat.
ranking.history: This diced salad is found throughout the eastern Mediterranean and is often called Arab salad in the Arab world. In the first half of the 20th century, settlers on kibbutzim (collective farms) made simple salads from the vegetables they grew themselves, served with breakfast eggs and cheese, making it part of Israeli food culture. Today it is almost a required side dish at every meal, and is also often stuffed into falafel and sabich.
